didYouKnow: The Glasgow Subway opened on 14 December 1896, making it the third-oldest underground metro in the world after London (1863) and Budapest (1896).
It is one of the very few railways with a 4 ft (1,219 mm) gauge, and its 11 ft (3.4 m) tunnels are smaller than London's deep tubes.
The Subway was cable-hauled until 1935 - a steam engine between West Street and Shields Road drove endless cables, one per direction.
On opening day a car carrying 60 passengers was hit by another beneath the Clyde; four were injured and the line was shut until 19 January 1897.
The circle is 10.5 km (6.5 miles) long and has never been extended - the only metro never to grow.
The line passes under the Clyde twice and the River Kelvin once; the Clyde crossings were driven under compressed air with gradients of about 1 in 18 and 1 in 20.
The shallowest point of the circle is only about 7 ft (2 m) below the surface, between Kinning Park and Cessnock; the deepest, near Hillhead, is about 155 ft (47 m).
Stations were laid out at the summit of roughly a 1 in 40 grade, so trains climb into each platform and drop out of it.
Until the 1977-80 rebuild, trains were lifted by crane onto the rails at Govan; Broomloan Depot now has a ramp to the tunnels.
Nicknames: the 'Clockwork Orange' (orange 1980s livery) and, before that, the 'Shoogly Train'.
In 1977 cracks in the roof of Govan Cross station closed the whole system eight days early.
St Enoch's red sandstone Flemish Renaissance building (James Miller, 1896) was lifted onto a concrete platform while the station beneath it was rebuilt.
Merkland Street station is the system's only 'ghost station' - drivers pass through the humped, wider tunnel where it used to be.
A German bomb damaged both tunnels near Merkland Street on 18 September 1940.
The new Stadler trains are 4-car, 39 m long and ready for driverless operation, entering service on 11 December 2023.
The 'Subcrawl' is a pub crawl with one drink at each of the 15 stations.
Cessnock's entrance is in a tenement basement beside a Greek Thomson building, and it still has its pre-1977 signage.
Kelvinbridge is the deepest station and its pumps run continuously against seepage from the River Kelvin.
